name: Disaggregated Prefill
question: Why make prefill and decode share a GPU?
summary: Inference has two phases with different needs. Prefill processes the whole prompt at once and is compute-bound; decode produces one token at a time and is limited by memory bandwidth. Running them on separate GPU pools and handing the KV cache across stops long prompts from stalling other users’ token streams, and lets each pool be sized and tuned on its own.
useCases: High-traffic serving with long prompts and many concurrent streams
Strict targets for both time to first token and tokens per second
Large deployments where GPU utilization matters

items.detail: compute-bound; sets time to first token (TTFT)
memory-bound; sets time per output token (TPOT)
cache moved from prefill to decode workers over fast links
tune the prefill-to-decode GPU ratio to traffic

steps: Measure TTFT and TPOT separately under real load
Consider disaggregation when long prompts and many streams compete
Use a fast interconnect (NVLink, RDMA) for KV transfer
Rebalance the prefill-to-decode ratio as traffic shifts
pitfalls: KV transfer adds network overhead and complexity
Little benefit for small models or light traffic
More components to operate and monitor
remember: Compute-heavy prefill, memory-heavy decode: split them.
caption: On a shared GPU the long prefill blocks decoding. Separate pools keep tokens flowing.

tpot = [(r.done_at - r.first_token_at) / (r.out_tokens - 1) for r in reqs]

steps.title: Measure TTFT and TPOT separately
steps.text: Averages hide the problem. On shared GPUs, p95 time to first token is 2.2 s and p95 time per output token is 61 ms, above a 50 ms target.

steps.title: See the interference
steps.text: A 30,000-token prefill occupies a GPU for about 1.5 s. Every stream decoding on that GPU waits: 1.5 s ÷ 30 ms = 50 tokens it could have produced.

steps.title: Split into two pools
steps.text: Prefill runs on its own GPUs, which are compute-bound. Decode runs on the others, which are limited by memory bandwidth. Here 2 and 6 of 8 GPUs.

steps.title: Hand over the KV cache
steps.text: The finished prompt’s KV cache moves to a decode GPU. For an 8B model with 8 KV heads that is 128 KiB per token, about 3.9 GB, roughly 80 ms over 400 Gb/s RDMA.

steps.title: Decode stays steady
steps.text: No prefill ever lands in the decode pool, so p95 TPOT falls to about 35 ms while the long prompts are still processed.

steps.title: Rebalance as traffic shifts
steps.text: If TTFT breaches its target while TPOT has room, move a GPU to prefill; if TPOT breaches, move one back to decode.

playgroundGuide.scenario: Eight GPUs serve 200 live chats while users upload long documents, each a 30,000-token prompt that takes 1.5 s of prefill on a dedicated GPU. The service promises p95 time to first token (TTFT) of at most 2.5 s and p95 time per output token (TPOT) of at most 50 ms. The latency figures come from a simple illustrative model, not a benchmark.
controls: Drag how many long prompts arrive per minute.
Choose shared GPUs or separate prefill and decode pools, and size the prefill pool.
Choose the link that carries each 3.9 GB KV cache from prefill to decode.

outputs.name: p95 TTFT
outputs.meaning: Queueing plus prefill, plus KV transfer when pools are split.

outputs.name: p95 TPOT
outputs.meaning: Decode speed per stream, including stalls from prefills on the same GPU.

presets.name: Shared GPUs
presets.expect: 20 uploads a minute on shared GPUs: TTFT 2.21 s passes, but prefills steal 6% of GPU time and TPOT is 61 ms, over the target.

presets.name: Split pools
presets.expect: 2 prefill and 6 decode GPUs over RDMA: TTFT 2.33 s (including 79 ms of KV transfer) and TPOT 35 ms. Both targets met.

presets.name: Slow link
presets.expect: Same split over 25 Gb Ethernet: each KV transfer takes 1.26 s, so TTFT rises to 3.51 s and misses its target.

presets.name: Light load
presets.expect: 4 uploads a minute on shared GPUs: TTFT 2.00 s and TPOT 37 ms. Both targets met without splitting.

missions.text: Meet both targets with at least 20 long prompts per minute.
missions.hint: Separate the pools and keep enough GPUs on each side.

missions.text: With split pools, break the TTFT target while TPOT stays within target.
missions.hint: Give the prefill pool too few GPUs for the upload rate.

missions.text: Find a load of at least 8 uploads a minute where shared GPUs meet both targets.
missions.hint: Stay on shared GPUs and lower the upload rate until TPOT drops under 50 ms.

goals: Explain why prefill is compute-bound and decode is memory-bandwidth-bound
Calculate token stalls and KV transfer times
Decide when disaggregation is worth its operational cost

practice.scenario: A large chat service receives long document uploads (30,000-token prompts) alongside thousands of ongoing chats. Moving prefill to its own GPU pool keeps everyone else's replies streaming smoothly while the documents are processed.

industries.use: Serve long prompts and many streams on the same fleet
Ingest long files without slowing live chat
Scale prompt-heavy and generation-heavy traffic separately

practice.analogy: A restaurant with a prep kitchen. The big catering order is prepped in the back without stopping the plates going out front.

library.name: NVIDIA Dynamo
library.what: Open-source serving framework for disaggregated prefill and decode, KV-aware routing and cache transfer, on top of engines such as vLLM.

practice.note: Conceptual sketch of what disaggregated serving frameworks do. Their APIs change quickly, so follow the framework’s own examples to deploy.

samples.code:
# Conceptual flow implemented by NVIDIA Dynamo, llm-d or vLLM's disaggregated mode

async def handle(request):
    prefill = least_loaded(PREFILL_POOL)            # compute-heavy GPUs
    kv, first_token = await prefill.run(request.prompt)

    decode = least_loaded(DECODE_POOL)              # memory-bandwidth-heavy GPUs
    await decode.receive_kv(kv)                     # transfer over NVLink / RDMA
    yield first_token
    async for token in decode.generate(max_tokens=request.max_tokens):
        yield token

# Scale each pool from its own metric:
#   time to first token too high   -> add prefill workers
#   time per output token too high -> add decode workers

numericDrill.question: Prefill of a 30k-token prompt takes 1.5 s. Decode produces a token every 30 ms. On a shared GPU, how many tokens could each waiting stream have produced during one prefill?
numericDrill.answer: 1.5 s ÷ 0.03 s = 50 tokens of stall per stream, which users see as a stutter. Separate pools remove it.

interview.question: Why are prefill and decode bottlenecked differently?
interview.answer: Prefill processes all prompt tokens in parallel, so it's limited by compute. Decode produces one token per step and must read the model weights and KV cache each time, so it's limited by memory bandwidth.

interview.question: What does disaggregation cost you?
interview.answer: Moving the KV cache between GPUs adds network traffic and latency, needs fast interconnects, and adds components to deploy, route and monitor. It pays off at high traffic with long prompts.

mistakes.fix: Track time to first token and time per output token separately, at p95

mistakes.mistake: Disaggregating a small, lightly loaded service
mistakes.fix: Use it when long prompts and many streams compete

quiz.question: What mainly limits the prefill phase?
quiz.explanation: All prompt tokens are processed in parallel, so prefill is compute-bound.

quiz.question: What mainly limits the decode phase?
quiz.explanation: Each new token requires reading the weights and KV cache, so decode is memory-bandwidth-bound.

quiz.question: A 20,000-token prompt takes 1.2 s to prefill on a GPU where streams decode at 40 ms per token. How many tokens could each waiting stream have produced during that prefill?
quiz.explanation: 1.2 s ÷ 0.04 s = 30 tokens of stall.

quiz.question: Which symptom most suggests disaggregated prefill would help?
options: p95 time per output token spikes whenever long documents are uploaded, while TTFT is fine
All requests are slow at night
quiz.explanation: Long prefills interfering with decode is exactly the problem it solves.

quiz.question: What does a disaggregated deployment need? Select all that apply.
options: A fast interconnect between prefill and decode GPUs
A way to transfer KV caches
A router that picks a prefill and a decode worker
quiz.explanation: Splitting phases adds transfer and routing; model size is unrelated.

quiz.question: A model has 32 layers, 8 KV heads and head dimension 128, stored in 16-bit precision. How much KV cache does one token need?
quiz.explanation: 2 (K and V) × 32 × 8 × 128 × 2 bytes = 131,072 bytes = 128 KiB.

quiz.question: At 128 KiB per token, a 10,000-token prompt’s KV cache is about 1.31 GB. How long does it take to move over a 50 GB/s link?
In a split deployment, p95 TTFT misses its target while p95 TPOT has plenty of room. What do you change?
options: Add prefill capacity, for example by moving a GPU from decode
quiz.explanation: TTFT is set by the prefill pool.

quiz.question: Which are signs you do not need disaggregation yet? Select all that apply.
options: A small model on a single GPU
p95 TPOT spikes whenever long prompts arrive
quiz.explanation: Spikes caused by long prompts are the reason to consider it.

quiz.question: What is the core idea of DistServe?
options: Run prefill and decode on different GPUs and tune each for its own latency target
quiz.explanation: It optimizes goodput under separate TTFT and TPOT targets.

quiz.question: Which metrics should you track for a disaggregated service? Select all that apply.
quiz.explanation: Averages hide the per-phase behaviour you are tuning.

quiz.question: Which technique reduces decode stalls on a shared GPU without separate pools?
options: Chunked prefill: long prompts are processed in pieces interleaved with decode steps
quiz.explanation: Chunking bounds how long any decode step waits, at some cost to TTFT.

quiz.question: 8 GPUs serve 200 streams with 2 prefill and 6 decode GPUs. If you move to 3 prefill GPUs, how many streams does each decode GPU serve?
quiz.explanation: 200 ÷ 5 = 40 streams per decode GPU, so TPOT will rise a little.

quiz.question: What did Splitwise propose beyond splitting the phases?
options: Running each phase on hardware suited to it, such as different GPU types
Training a new model per phase
quiz.explanation: Decode needs less compute, so older or cheaper GPUs can serve it efficiently.

quiz.question: Mooncake, a KV-cache-centric disaggregated architecture, was built to serve which product?
quiz.explanation: Its paper describes serving Kimi with a disaggregated, KV-cache-centric design.

quiz.question: What are the downsides of disaggregated serving? Select all that apply.
options: More components to deploy and monitor
The prefill-to-decode ratio needs ongoing tuning
quiz.explanation: Outputs are identical; the costs are operational.

quiz.question: A response has 401 output tokens. The first token arrives at 2.0 s and the last at 14.0 s. What is its TPOT?
Why not simply add more GPUs to the shared pool instead of splitting it?
options: Each long prefill still interrupts every stream on the GPU it lands on; more GPUs only make it less frequent
Splitting needs fewer GPUs in every case
quiz.explanation: Interference is structural in a shared pool; splitting removes it.

quiz.question: Which projects support prefill–decode disaggregation? Select all that apply.
quiz.explanation: tree-sitter is a code parser.

quiz.question: Prefill and decode nodes are joined by 10 Gb Ethernet, about 1.25 GB/s. A 3.9 GB KV cache must move for each long prompt. What should you conclude?
options: Transfer takes about 3.1 s, adding directly to TTFT: keep phases together or get a faster link
quiz.explanation: 3.9 ÷ 1.25 ≈ 3.1 s of extra TTFT per long prompt outweighs the benefit.
